strengths: Significance: The unified treatment of streaming Tucker-rank regression, completion, and binary observations addresses a useful problem. Updating from individual observations offers a clear storage advantage over repeatedly fitting all accumulated data.

Originality: The most promising contribution is the tensor-specific analysis, particularly the spectral-projector approach to preserving incoherence and controlling entrywise completion errors without trimming (Theorem 5 and Appendix D.2).

Presentation and empirical support: Algorithms 1–2 clearly specify the updates and step-size schedule. Figure 1 illustrates the predicted effects of step size and noise, including summaries from 10 independent trials.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript explicitly distinguishes refinement from initialization costs (p. 23) and acknowledges the restrictive binary-learning sample complexity and missing initialization guarantees (p. 27). The public MovieLens dataset is attributed; no material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—concentration argument: In Appendix D.1, p. 53, the purported martingale differences D_l and F_l multiply centered quantities by 1(E_l), but E_l depends on the current observation X_l. Such multiplication does not generally preserve zero conditional mean. The subsequent Azuma–Hoeffding application establishes neither the required martingale property nor a bound on the resulting truncation bias. This leaves the main high-probability argument for Theorem 1 incomplete.

Soundness—expected regret: Appendix D.4, pp. 83–84, uses an unconditional failure probability inside a conditional Cauchy–Schwarz argument to obtain Eqs. (85)–(86). The required conditional probability can equal one when an earlier iterate has left the local basin, because the event itself includes a local-error condition. Consequently, the contribution of these trajectories to expected loss is not controlled by the provided argument. This materially affects Theorems 7–8, including the headline logarithmic-regret claim.

Soundness—Poisson extension: Theorem 4’s proof (p. 21) bounds the Poisson response’s ψ1 norm by 10/log(1 + I exp(-α) log 2), which decreases with intensity I. For Y distributed as Poisson(I), the manuscript’s norm definition instead gives 1/log(1 + (log 2)/I), which grows with I. Thus the stated noise bound and resulting theorem conditions require rederivation.

Originality and claim calibration: Section 6 studies stochastic pseudo-regret against the population optimum under independent observations and warm initialization, rather than regret against a comparator selected after observing the realized losses. The cited Shi et al. and Zhou et al. papers concern tensor bandits, so their square-root regret bounds are not directly comparable. The broad claim of the first logarithmic regret for nonconvex functions (p. 31), and the optimality language, need a matched comparison and a rigorous lower-bound justification.

Evaluation: Section 8.3 tests only fixed-step-size square-root regret in a matrix problem; it does not evaluate Algorithm 2’s logarithmic regret. There are also no experiments on the generalized linear models, entrywise guarantees, or incoherence preservation. Runtime and memory measurements are absent despite computational efficiency being a central motivation.

Reproducibility: Although pseudocode and several simulation parameters are supplied, the manuscript provides no code link, initialization sample counts, or sufficient MovieLens preprocessing and step-size-selection details. These omissions impede reproducing the empirical results and assessing the total cost including initialization.

Presentation: Repeated interpretation paragraphs on pp. 17–18, inconsistent Poisson model and loss formulas in Example 3 and Section 3.3, and the unfinished sentence 'Notice we can set .' on p. 86 hinder verification. The useful theoretical direction does not compensate for the unresolved proof gaps; substantial technical revision is needed before the central claims can be relied upon.
